title: RESTORATIVE EFFECTS OF NATURAL ENVIRONMENT EXPERIENCES
research_question: Do experiences in natural environments have restorative effects on emotional states, cognitive performance, and physiological measures, compared to urban environments, nonwilderness vacations, or passive relaxation?

participants.description: Study 1: 68 experienced, physically fit backpackers (35.9-31.6 years mean age across groups, 56-64% male) from California. Study 2: 102 college students (M=20 years, 17 men, 17 women per condition) from introductory social science courses.
participants.recruitment: Study 1: Wilderness group recruited at trailheads in California's Sierra Nevada mountains. Control groups from local outing clubs, Sierra Club members, and referrals. Study 2: College students participated in exchange for course credit.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Study 1: Extended wilderness backpacking trip (4-7 days), nonwilderness vacation (4-7 days, e.g., car touring, family visits, sightseeing), or normal daily routines at home in Los Angeles-Orange County metropolitan area. Study 2: 40-minute walk in a natural park setting (Santiago Oaks Regional Park, Orange, CA), 40-minute walk in an urban setting (Santa Ana, CA), or 40-minute passive relaxation in a laboratory setting (comfortable chair, magazines, radio, reading lamp).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Methods sections for Study 1 and Study 2

20-item Likert-type scale (measuring fascination, being away, coherence/extent, compatibility)
Psyonics AGSC device with Beckman 16 mm silver-silver chloride electrodes
5-point rating scale and frequency of aerobic workouts

mechanisms: Reduction of mental fatigue by restoring directed attention capacity through involuntary attention (fascination).
Reduction of arousal and blocking of negatively toned feelings by nontaxing natural stimuli.
Proactive effects of restorative experiences, preparing individuals to better cope with daily stress and strain.
Natural settings provide a sense of being away, extent, and compatibility, which are key to restoration.
implementation_implications: Carefully constructed therapeutic environments, including urban parks and wilderness areas, may facilitate recovery from mental fatigue.
Natural environments may have proactive effects, 'inoculating' people against stress and attentional demands.
Designers should consider incorporating elements that elicit fascination, provide a sense of being away and extent, and are compatible with user purposes.

limitations: Study 1: Quasi-experimental design with self-selection into groups, though mitigated by controls (experienced backpackers, fitness assessment, covariates).
Study 1: Limited external validity due to restricted population sampling (experienced, physically fit backpackers).
Study 1: Proofreading measure not repeated at follow-up due to administration difficulty.
Study 1: Significance level set at p = .10 due to exploratory nature and field study conditions (minimal control over extraneous variation, decreased statistical power).
Study 1: Mixed feelings immediately following wilderness experience, potentially masking positive affect due to return to daily demands.
Study 2: Physiological measures (blood pressure, heart rate) showed no significant differences, possibly due to procedural cause (not monitored during treatment, assessments 50 minutes post-task).
Study 2: Perceived restorativeness scale is in initial stage of development, tested with modest sample and limited range of settings.
General: The importance of temporal factors (e.g., timing of measurements) in wilderness experiences needs more careful monitoring.
General: The 'being away' factor alone is not sufficient for restorative effects; other factors are critical.

paper_metadata.title: Restorative Effects of Natural Environment Experiences
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Restorative Effects of Natural Environment Experiences
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The utility of different theoretical models of restorative experience was explored in a quasi-experimental field study and a true experiment. The former included wilderness backpacking and nonwilderness vacation conditions, as well as a control condition in which participants continued with their daily routines. The latter had urban environment, natural environment, and passive relaxation conditions. Multimethod assessments of restoration consisted of self-reports of affective states, cognitive performance, and, in the latter study, physiological measures. Convergent self-report and performance results obtained in both studies offer evidence of greater restorative effects arising from experiences in nature. Implications for theory, methodology, and design are discussed.
